To overrate something means to judge it as better, more important, more talented, or more valuable than it actually is. Your opinion of it is higher than the truth supports.
A simple way to picture it

Imagine a rating scale from 1 to 10. A movie genuinely deserves a 5 — it's average. But you give it a 9 because you loved it. You have overrated it. Your judgment is inflated beyond what reality justifies.
"Over" means too much. "Rate" means to judge the quality or value of something. Put them together: to overrate = to judge something too highly. That's the entire logic of the word.
How to use it in a sentence

The person doing the judging is the subject, and the thing being judged too highly is the object.

  • She overrates her singing ability. (She believes she sings better than she actually does.)
  • Critics overrated that film. (Critics praised it more than it deserved.)
  • People overrate the importance of being busy. (They place more value on busyness than it truly deserves.)
Almost anything: a person's talent, a film, a book, a restaurant, a place, a strategy, a product, or even an idea. If something can be judged, it can be overrated.

Overrating is always a mistake in judgment, not a lie. The person who overrates something genuinely believes their high opinion — they are simply wrong. They are not trying to deceive anyone; they have misjudged. This is what separates overrating from flattery or dishonesty.

In everyday English, you will most frequently see the past participle form overrated, used as an adjective to describe the thing being misjudged.

  • That restaurant is overrated. = People think it is better than it actually is.
  • He is overrated as a footballer. = His reputation is bigger than his actual ability.
  • The holiday was overrated. = It did not live up to the high expectations people had set for it.

This form is extremely common — arguably more common than the base verb form in casual conversation.

The mirror image of overrate is underrate — to think something is less good, less capable, or less valuable than it actually is.

  • People underrate this book. = It is better than most people think.
  • She underrates herself. = She thinks she is worse than she actually is.

Knowing the opposite sharpens your understanding of both words: overrating pushes your judgment above reality, underrating pushes it below reality.
Where you will encounter this word

Overrate and overrated are extremely common in discussions about sports ("He is one of the most overrated players in the league"), films and music ("That album is massively overrated"), food and travel ("People overrate that city as a tourist destination"), and self-assessment ("Don't overrate your chances").

To overrate = to think too highly of something. The gap between how good you think something is and how good it actually is — that gap is what overrating describes. It is always an error of judgment, never an act of deception, and it can apply to anything in the world that is capable of being assessed.
